newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spacewoman greeted with candy on return.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spacewoman greeted with candy on return.

text.p: After 188 days in orbit on a Russian space station, NASA endurance champion Shannon Lucid returned to Earth on Thursday and celebrated with a box of M&M candies sent by President Bill Clinton.
The $2 billion shuttle Atlantis slipped through the Florida morning sky and touched down at Kennedy Space Centre at 8:13 a.m. EDT (1213 GMT).

National Aeronautics and Space Administration chief Daniel Goldin welcomed Lucid back to Earth with a large box of M&Ms from Clinton. "I've never seen a box of M&Ms with the presidental seal on top of it," he told reporters.
During the flight, Lucid expressed her craving for the candy and had packets of M&Ms delivered to Mir aboard unmanned cargo craft.
Clinton later made a telephone call to congratulate Lucid on the successful end of the mission.

"You've been a terrific inspiration for young women around the country and all around the world," he said. "You've given us all a great deal to be proud of and a lot of thrills. We're glad you're home safe and sound."
The president also checked to make sure she had received her M&Ms.
Lucid replied, "That was so nice and so thoughtful of you. Really, really appreciate that."

She rode home in a reclining seat designed to cushion her from the effects of gravity. After six months in weightlessness, the 53-year-old biochemist was expected to feel weak and woozy, NASA doctors said.

"Welcome home, Shannon, from your record-setting mission," spacecraft communicator Bill Gregory radioed from mission control in Houston as the shuttle came to a halt on the three-mile-long (4.8-km-long) runway.
The touchdown marked the end of a 75-million-mile (121-million-km) voyage for Lucid, who spent six months performing scientific research aboard Russia's Mir space station.

"There is an acute recovery during the first few days where she gets her land legs back, so to speak," said Dr. Roger Billica, chief of medical operations at Johnson Space Centre in Houston. "That's followed by a two-to-three-week period of a very active rehabilitation programme."
Within an hour of landing, Lucid and her five crewmates left Atlantis and boarded a special transport vehicle.
"She came out of the shuttle on her own power, but I think a couple of people just were holding onto her just to make sure she wouldn't fall," NASA Administrator Goldin said.
Dr Gaylen Johnson, the surgeon who monitored Lucid's health from Earth throughout her flight, earlier boarded the shuttle on the runway to gauge the astronaut's condition.

A team of physicians, physical therapists, trainers, dieticians and psychologists are standing by to assist Lucid over the next few weeks if necessary. Her six-month stay in space was the longest by an American and a record for a woman.
"The docs say that she is in really good health, that there are no surprises and they expect her rehabilitation to go normal," said Frank Culbertson, who heads NASA's shuttle-Mir programme.
The Atlantis astronauts were expected to stay in Florida overnight and return to their homes in Houston on Friday. Lucid may be allowed home on Friday night, accompanied by a doctor.

The veteran spacewoman, who joined NASA in 1978, was the first of six astronauts who will staff the remote Russian space outpost into 1998. Her place on Mir was taken by astronaut John Blaha, a 54-year-old Vietnam veteran.
Atlantis left him at the station for a four-month tour of duty with Russian cosmonauts Valeri Korzun and Alexander Kaleri. The shuttle will return to Mir in January for another change of crew.
